I’d like to share a tip for getting more practice building with AI — that is, either using AI building blocks to build applications or using AI coding assistance to create powerful applications quickly: If you find yourself with only limited time to build, reduce the scope of your project until you can build something in whatever time you do have.

If you have only an hour, find a small component of an idea that you're excited about that you can build in an hour. With modern coding assistants like Anthropic’s Claude Code (my favorite dev tool right now), you might be surprised at how much you can do even in short periods of time! This gets you going, and you can always continue the project later.

To become good at building with AI, most people must (i) learn relevant techniques, for example by taking online AI courses, and (ii) practice building. I know developers who noodle on ideas for months without actually building anything — I’ve done this too! — because we feel we don’t have time to get started. If you find yourself in this position, I encourage you to keep cutting the initial project scope until you identify a small component you can build right away.

Let me illustrate with an example — one of my many small, fun weekend projects that might never go anywhere, but that I’m glad I did.

Here’s the idea: Many people fear public speaking. And public speaking is challenging to practice, because it's hard to organize an audience. So I thought it would be interesting to build an audience simulator to provide a digital audience of dozens to hundreds of virtual people on a computer monitor and let a user practice by speaking to them.

One Saturday afternoon, I found myself in a coffee shop with a couple of hours to spare and decided to give the audience simulator a shot. My familiarity with graphics coding is limited, so instead of building a complex simulator of a large audience and writing AI software to simulate appropriate audience responses, I decided to cut scope significantly to (a) simulating an audience of one person (which I could replicate later to simulate N persons), (b) omitting AI and letting a human operator manually select the reaction of the simulated audience (similar to Wizard of Oz prototyping), and (c) implementing the graphics using a simple 2D avatar.

Using a mix of several coding assistants, I built a basic version in the time I had. The avatar could move subtly and blink, but otherwise it used basic graphics. Even though it fell far short of a sophisticated audience simulator, I am glad I built this. In addition to moving the project forward and letting me explore different designs, it advanced my knowledge of basic graphics. Further, having this crude prototype to show friends helped me get user feedback that shaped my views on the product idea.

Here are the top AI tools for marketers right now

Personally, my list only has ONE tool and it's because 99.9% of my time is spent with my friend ChatGPT. Just strolling through the woods in Vermont talking to my little robot. I know, I know.

But we happen to run the top community for a huge group of marketing professionals, so I took to the streets (aka the message boards) to ask the Exit Five community their most used AI tools right now.

No affiliations with any of these companies, not getting paid to post this; truly a finger on the pulse type of thing - here are the 15 tools that come up the most in Exit Five right now.

1. ChatGPT / Custom GPTs

The catch-all workhorse. Campaign names. Research. Outlines. Internal playbooks. If you haven’t already: build a brand-trained GPT that gives you 20 campaign name options in seconds. Helps me go from 0 to 1 faster. Get the bad ideas out of the system.

2. Claude

They say it's better for long documents and repurposing. Drop in your last year of content and get a pattern analysis you definitely weren’t going to do manually. I just like the name. Claude.

3. Canva Magic Studio

Canva rocks. When you need designer-level output… without a designer. Spin up carousels, ads, and visuals in minutes. Even makes me look good.

4. Descript

Edit video like a doc. Cut filler. Pull clips. Export. Done in a fraction of the time.

5. Perplexity

Your research intern. Competitor tracking. Trend scans. Summary + sources.
Great when someone Slacks you “quick question” and you need to look prepared. Do you all like this better than Google? Than ChatGPT? It's different? How

6. SurferSEO

SEO briefs and optimization that make ranking feel less like a gamble. Great name btw.

7. Ahrefs + Frase

Find old posts losing traffic. Patch the gaps. Win back rankings.

8. Make

Lead routing and follow-up workflows that run while you sleep.

9. Zapier (+ Agents)

Reporting, notifications, cross-tool workflows. Everything that used to require ops help.

10. Clay

List building and enrichment on autopilot.
Find contacts. Pull data. Build prospect lists that would've taken days.

11. ElevenLabs

Voice cloning for audio versions of your content. You type. “You” talks. I want to use this for our podcast ads but I think the real mean sounds more authentic?

12. Vercel V0

Landing pages that practically build themselves, with auto A/B tests baked in.

13. Flourish

Data visuals and interactive maps that make your spreadsheet look like a crime scene. Uh. OK? Is that a good thing?

14. GenSpark

Upload data. Get insights and a deck. No more begging for analytics support.

15. NotebookLM

Drop in transcripts, internal docs, and case studies. Get messaging ideas, customer language, objections, topics - all from your own data.

Leave me a comment if you have a favorite tool on this list (or a use case we didn’t put down here or want to answer one of my Qs)

Breaking Down AI: Basic Concepts Every Professional Should Know

The world of AI can seem overwhelming, but understanding its fundamental concepts is crucial. 

Let me break down the core elements:

Key Components of Modern AI:

Artificial Intelligence(AI) sits at the top - the broad umbrella encompassing systems designed to mimic human cognition.

Machine Learning flows from AI, where algorithms improve through data exposure and experience. Think of it like a student getting better with practice.

Deep Learning takes it further, using complex neural networks to excel at pattern recognition - similar to how our brains process information.

Practical Applications:

- Speech Recognition powers your daily voice assistants
- Computer Vision enables facial recognition and autonomous vehicles
- Natural Language Processing drives chatbots and language translation
- Reinforcement Learning helps systems learn optimal actions through trial and error
- Supervised Learning uses labeled data to make predictions
- Unsupervised Learning discovers hidden patterns without predefined labels

The beauty of modern AI lies in its versatility - from healthcare diagnostics to financial forecasting; these technologies are reshaping how we work and live.

Why This Matters:
Understanding these concepts isn't just for tech professionals. As AI becomes integrated into every industry, this knowledge helps you make informed decisions about implementing AI solutions in your work.

AI is only as powerful as the data it learns from. But raw data alone isn’t enough—it needs to be collected, processed, structured, and analyzed before it can drive meaningful AI applications.  

How does data transform into AI-driven insights? Here’s the data journey that powers modern AI and analytics:  

1. 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 – AI models need diverse inputs: structured data (databases, spreadsheets) and unstructured data (text, images, audio, IoT streams). The challenge is managing high-volume, high-velocity data efficiently.  

2. 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 – AI thrives on accessibility. Whether on AWS, Azure, PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Amazon S3, scalable storage ensures real-time access to training and inference data.  

3. 𝗘𝗧𝗟 (𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁, 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺, 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗱) – Dirty data leads to bad AI decisions. Data engineers build ETL pipelines that clean, integrate, and optimize datasets before feeding them into AI and machine learning models.  

4. 𝗔𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 – Data lakes and warehouses such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift prepare and stage data, making it easier for AI to recognize patterns and generate predictions.  

5. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 – AI doesn’t work in silos. Well-structured dimension tables, fact tables, and Elasticube models help establish relationships between data points, enhancing model accuracy.  

6. 𝗔𝗜-𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 – The final step is turning data into intelligent, real-time business decisions with BI dashboards, NLP, machine learning, and augmented analytics.  

AI without the right data strategy is like a high-performance engine without fuel. A well-structured data pipeline enhances model performance, ensures accuracy, and drives automation at scale.  

How are you optimizing your data pipeline for AI? What challenges do you face when integrating AI into your business? Let’s discuss.
